claim: Blending (find a shared generic space, then build a blend with emergent properties) is the hardest of association, analogy and blending for 35 LLMs: valid rate 43.4% vs 53.4% (analogy) and 59.0% (association). Humans (Prolific, N=75) were lower still on blends (12.8%).
agent_test: Run the open-mode blend operator on KOMBINE-style random pairs at equal tokens: plain 'combine these' prompt vs forced generic-space-then-blend; count valid blends by a code check for non-vacuous shared property.

claim: The weak step in LLM blending appears to be choosing the bridge or shared abstraction, not building the blend. KOMBINE: valid generic space 43.4%, but 97.1% coherent blends once one is valid. PopBlends: connecting concept judged right 56.7% of the time, but given a strong connecting concept at least one generated scene relates to it 98.3% of the time. Ge and Parikh 2021 found larger language models propose better linking properties than smaller ones and than ConceptNet (precision rises with model size).
agent_test: Split the operator into (1) state a generic frame that fits both inputs, checked by code or by a second blind call for non-vacuity, (2) project and elaborate. Compare with one-shot blending at equal tokens; measure the share of vacuous frames caught.
audit_note: KOMBINE 43.4/97.1 and PopBlends 56.7 are right, but PopBlends' 98.3% is the chance that at least one generated scene relates to a strong connecting concept (possibly only one domain), not 98.3% of scenes on-topic; Ge and Parikh show larger LMs give higher precision but do not say the property-finding step is the limiting step.
claim_before_audit: The weak step in LLM blending is choosing the bridge or shared abstraction, not building the blend. KOMBINE: valid generic space 43.4%, but 97.1% coherent blends once one is valid. PopBlends: connecting concept right 56.7%, but 98.3% of scenes then on-topic. Ge and Parikh 2021: the find-the-shared-property step improves with model scale and is the limiting step.

claim: Blends from different LLMs repeat each other far more than analogies: 37.3% vs 2.6% of invented concepts share 2 or more near-identical properties (14.3x); 94.7% vs 36.3% at 1 or more. Same-provider models are 2.3x more likely to coincide (9.3% vs 4.1%). One in five invented concepts overall (412/2,070) is a repeat.
agent_test: Draw 10 blends from the same model for one pair, then 10 blends from 10 different input pairs sharing the same generic frame; count distinct emergent properties by embedding threshold at equal tokens.

claim: LLM ideation collapses in diversity even when individual ideas look novel: Si et al. found only about 5% non-duplicate ideas among 4,000 seeds per topic (cosine 0.8) while blind experts rated AI ideas more novel (5.64 vs 4.84) but not more feasible; KOMBINE found the same collapse on blends.
agent_test: Dedupe candidate blends in code by embedding similarity before selection; measure unique-blend yield per 1,000 tokens with and without input-pair variation.
audit_note: Si numbers match (5%, 4000 seeds per topic, 5.64 vs 4.84, feasibility n.s.). 'KOMBINE found the same collapse' is loose: KOMBINE reports cross-model repetition (19.9% of concepts, 37.3% on blends), a milder and different measure than Si's 5% non-duplicates.

claim: Adding an explicit shared-attribute or abstraction step before combining improves blend quality beyond a longer prompt, but the evidence is partial. IEI (image models): ranking improved for all five models (Friedman p<0.0001) while prompt length did not differ (487.95 vs 514.53 words, p=.404). Schema-driven transfer (invariant kept fixed, carrier swapped) beat a strong single prompt on human ratings (e.g. ingenuity 4.56 vs 3.69), not at equal tokens. CCPT (corrected in evidence d01): spreading activation raised GPT-4o emergent-property score from 40.8 to 45.8 (+5.0), chain-of-thought to 42.4 (+1.6); the 57.8 figure is a best-of-5 oracle row, not the scaffold. One protocol-vs-brainstorming case (74/80 vs 49/80) uses an AI judge and unmatched tokens (d08).
agent_test: Compare three arms at equal tokens on a blend benchmark: plain prompt; chain-of-thought; expand-both-inputs then state shared attributes then blend. Score emergent property validity by code against the input property lists. Note: CCPT shows a small scaffold gain (+5) and a large best-of-5 gain (+17), so include a best-of-N arm.

claim: Most of the gain from blend scaffolding comes from a single well-written blending template; extra stages (transfer agent, diagnostic backtracking) add smaller increments. Beyond Pixels human ratings: Direct 2.75, Strong prompt 3.69, w/o diagnostic 4.05, full 4.56 on ingenuity.
agent_test: Test single-pass template vs template plus one diagnose-and-retry round at equal tokens; keep the retry only if it pays (G7).

claim: Truly emergent attributes are rare in plain human conceptual conjunction: 3 of 174 attributes under strict scoring (11 lenient) in Hampton 1987; none in Hampson trait pairs (31 of 32 inherited when congruent); under a negated constituent only 6 of 51 reached 10% or more. Most apparent emergence is recall of known instances or category stretching.
agent_test: For each blend the agent proposes, code checks that the claimed emergent property is absent from both source property lists and not a restatement; report how often claimed emergence fails this check.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-31 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Emergence is higher when the combination is incongruent and the reader must explain it: social stereotype conjunctions gave emergent ratings on 23% (congruent) and 33% (incongruent) of ratings; people explained contradictions by recalling a case, applying a rule, or simulating. Perspective changes the blend: 17% of own-view attributes but 69% of other-category attributes were inherited; 35% of attributes false of both parts were judged true of the conjunction.
agent_test: Ask the operator 'why could these two coexist' vs a plain merge prompt; compare validity of emergent claims at equal tokens. Run each blend under two stated perspectives and count disagreement.

claim: Making the two inputs more distant raises emergence or novelty in human conceptual combination (Estes and Ward 2002, Wilkenfeld and Ward 2001; abstracts and second-hand only) but not reliably creativity or quality. Chan, Dow and Schunn (opened): 707 concepts citing sources on 12 challenges, shortlist rate fell with source distance (-0.33 log-odds per unit, 95% CI -0.06 to -0.60) and far sources did no better than citing nothing (0.09 shortlisted). Chan and Schunn 2015 (abstract): far analogies raised concept generation rate but concepts after them were more similar to the previous one. Kennedy 2015 (N=195): atypical seeds gave no creativity gain (F(1,193)=1.680). KOMBINE random unrelated pairs gave mostly invalid blends.
schema_part: O7 (far analogues only at impasses and open mode)
agent_test: Sweep input distance (embedding distance bins) at equal tokens; score validity and downstream usefulness of the blend, not only novelty.

claim: Building on a blend (iteration) beats a single far combination: indirect effects of far combinations (concepts built on them) were more consistently positive than direct effects in a large online innovation platform.
agent_test: Compare one-shot blend with blend then one refinement round against a check, at equal tokens.

claim: Processing metaphor and mapping-demanding literal sentences costs more than plain literal sentences, with a graded N400: Coulson and Van Petten (18 adults, 165 triplets, linear trend F(1,17)=6.86, p<.02); Lai et al. 2009 (29 adults) replicated the metaphor-over-literal cost with a conventionality time course (reaction times 1377, 1487, 1620 ms for literal, conventional, novel).
agent_test: Not an agent test. Use only to justify treating input distance as a controlled variable.
audit_note: Lai recruited 29 but the ANOVA dfs (69) imply 24 analysed; all quoted statistics and RTs match.

claim: ERP evidence does not discriminate blending from other accounts of semantic integration cost: authors of the replication read the pattern as consistent with indirect-access and career-of-metaphor accounts, and a review notes the blending ERP studies controlled cloze but not expression novelty and complexity.
agent_test: None. Do not cite ERP as proof of the four-space mechanism.

claim: Blending theory is contested as a testable theory: Gibbs (as reported by Ritchie 2004) questions how it could be tested or falsified, Harder objects that it adds needless complexity to simple processes, and Ritchie argues the four-space structure follows from metaphors rather than data and impedes testable hypotheses. Turner (2013) concedes blending theory is more a framework for a research program than a theory, that evidence so far is mostly generalisation over in-sample data tested on out-of-sample data, and that the process itself does not appear to be algorithmic, so computer models are only suggestive.
agent_test: Borrow only checkable outputs (stated generic frame, stated emergent claim, run result) and compare against a plain combine-two-ideas prompt at equal tokens; drop any blend step that does not win.
audit_note: Per Ritchie, Gibbs raised falsifiability and Harder raised needless complexity/scope (Harder is not a falsifiability critic); Glebkin could not be opened; Turner says blending is more a research-program framework than a theory and that the mental process does not appear algorithmic, not that it lacks a falsifiable hypothesis. a09 and b11 are the same Turner page.
claim_before_audit: Blending theory is a framework with no single falsifiable hypothesis and no algorithm: Gibbs, Harder, Ritchie, Glebkin raise this and Turner concedes the evidence is in-sample generalisation and the process 'does not appear to be algorithmic'. Four-space structure is not shown to be necessary.

claim: Model judges give only moderate agreement with humans when scoring blend quality and creativity: the KOMBINE panel agreed with one author 66% overall and 75% when unanimous (ICC 0.48 for blend emergent utility, 0.67 for other blend dimensions, though leaderboard ranking was stable); LLM judges of research ideas reached 43.3 to 53.3% accuracy vs human reviewer consistency of 56.1% (Si et al.). Human annotators on PopBlends connecting concepts also agreed only moderately (kappa .43).
agent_test: Select blends by code checks and by running (tests, constraints, unpacking: can both inputs be recovered); log how often a blind model judge agrees with the code selector.
audit_note: Numbers match (66%/75%, ICC 0.48, 43.3-53.3 vs 56.1, kappa .43), but Sato 2025 is a tone-modulation study whose only inconsistency is in its own phase-shift analysis, not model ratings of blend quality; KOMBINE itself calls panel ICC fair-to-good and leaderboard ranking stable; the PopBlends kappa is human-annotator reliability.
claim_before_audit: Model judges are unreliable for scoring blend quality and creativity: KOMBINE panel agrees with a human 66% overall and 75% when unanimous (ICC for emergent utility 0.48); LLM judges of research ideas reached 43.3 to 53.3% vs human reviewers 56.1%; PopBlends human annotators kappa .43; Sato found rating models inconsistent.

claim: Putting two concepts into one prompt is not integration: fused and non-fused prompts did not differ in elicited model tone (one-tailed Welch, fused vs non-fused n.s.; both beat control p<.05/.01; GPT-4o n=15, Gemini 2.5 Pro n=5), although the model could describe the contrast when asked. Sato's other paper offers no test.
agent_test: Check integration structurally (both frames present, emergent claim present, roles preserved) rather than by length or tone.

claim: A scaffold that proposes several bridging concepts and filters them is near-certain to include a good one: PopBlends best-of-five 93.3% (90.0 / 96.6 / 93.3 for No-, Half-, Full-GPT) vs single attempt 56.7%; tool users produced 2.03 ideas per pair vs 0.87 with web search (N=10, p<.001). Misty (N=14): mean satisfaction per LLM blend only 3.2/5. CCPT agrees: GPT-4o best-of-5 (Multi-Oracle) reaches emergent score 57.8 vs 40.8 for one sample (d01).
agent_test: Sample 5 bridges, rank in code, expand only the best; compare with one bridge and with 5 expanded blends at equal tokens.
audit_note: All numbers match (table label offset in extraction aside). Caveat: CCPT Multi-Oracle is an upper bound selected using the metric, not an achievable filter, and 56.7% is the per-concept rate rather than a strict top-1.

claim: LLMs recognise emergent properties better than they produce them: GPT-4o judges 'has property' 95.6% and 'lacks property' 69.6% (82.6% mean) but labels property type only 56.4% (human 81%; component 37.2% correct, canceled 45.2%). Generated emergent noun phrases score 20.4 (base) and 26.9 at best with a scaffold, vs human 38.0 and gold 59.9; in property induction GPT-4o scores 40.8 (base) vs human 49.2 and gold 58.4. (Corrected: earlier text gave a base of 23.1, which is the CoT row.)
agent_test: Generate emergent property claims, then verify each with a separate check call against both source property lists; measure false-emergent rate.

claim: In VMetaphor-Bench (11 text-to-image models), images prompted for replacement metaphors were identified as replacement structure only 18.9% of the time versus 67.9% for fusion and 69.2% for juxtaposition; switching from a conceptual to a detailed descriptive prompt raised MCQ accuracy by 3.1 to 16.6 points on the representative models. In the IEI visual-mashup study, 9 of 11 models identified fusion mashups with higher precision than replacement ones, which the authors say mirrors human patterns.
agent_test: In text blends, tell the operator which blend type to produce (fuse, replace, juxtapose) and compare validity per type at equal tokens.
audit_note: VMetaphor numbers (18.9/67.9/69.2, +3.1 to +16.6) match, but 18.9% is the judge's structure-type identification on generated images, and the descriptive prompt details the visual realization rather than naming the structure. IEI measured 11 models (fusion higher precision in 9; its Fig. 5 caption even says the opposite) and only says this mirrors human patterns, with no human replacement-vs-fusion measurement.
claim_before_audit: Replacement-type blends are harder than fusion or juxtaposition: VMetaphor-Bench accuracy 18.9% for replacement vs 67.9% fusion and 69.2% juxtaposition; naming the structure in a descriptive prompt adds 3.1 to 16.6 points. IEI: replacement mashups harder than fusion for humans.

claim: Blend outcome depends on how the inputs are weighted and ordered: interpolating two concept embeddings in Stable Diffusion gave blended depiction 0.621 at the midpoint but 0.389 averaged over all ratios (extremes about 0.14 to 0.26). In Olearo et al. (22 concept pairs, 100 participants), embedding interpolation was the least preferred of four blending methods overall (not for same-class pairs); it is order-symmetric, whereas the switching, alternating and U-Net methods are order-sensitive and often let the first concept dominate.
agent_test: For each text blend, run both input orders and compare; reject blends where one input dominates (one source supplies all properties).
audit_note: Matsuhira numbers match. Olearo et al.: embedding interpolation (TEXTUAL) was least preferred overall (but not in the Same-class category), and it is the only symmetric method, so order effects and first-concept dominance belong to SWITCH/ALTERNATE/UNET, not to interpolation.
claim_before_audit: Blend outcome depends on how the inputs are weighted and ordered: interpolating two concept embeddings in Stable Diffusion gave blended depiction 0.621 at the midpoint but 0.389 averaged over all ratios (extremes about 0.14 to 0.26); in another test, embedding interpolation was the worst method, the first concept dominated, and order mattered.

claim: Blends can arise without explicit four-space structure (embedding averaging in diffusion, deep networks), which supports the critique that simpler processes may explain blends; no test pits structured blending against an averaging or plain-association baseline for text.
agent_test: Run a plain 'combine X and Y' arm vs the structured blend arm at equal tokens; keep the structure only if it wins on validity.

claim: Retrieving analogues at several abstraction levels before recombining gives ideas closer to what authors actually did: similarity 0.85 vs 0.78, 0.83 vs 0.75, 0.87 vs 0.77 (87 papers, one model); evidence is thin (embedding similarity only, no human raters).
agent_test: Level-by-level retrieval of the generic frame vs direct generation, scored by held-out outcome rather than similarity.

claim: The best model for blending differs from the best for association and analogy, and association originality predicts blending ability (r=0.42 originality, r=0.48 valid blend; leader on blends gpt-5.6-sol 64.8, leader on association and analogy claude-opus-4.6). LLMs and humans occupy different regions of semantic space.
agent_test: Evaluate candidate models on the blend operator separately from the main reasoner.

claim: Giving LLMs an explicit goal plus a test of the blend improves their blends over free combination, because human blends are goal-selected; this is a conceptual proposal with a toy model only.
agent_test: Blend with a stated goal and required affordances, test against it, revise from failure; compare with goal-free blending at equal tokens.

claim: Temperature is a weak lever for creative output. Llama-2-chat 70B stories: temperature predicted rated novelty only weakly (beta .308, SE .138) and incoherence moderately (beta .240), with no effect on typicality or cohesion (36 raters, 31 stories, 100 stories per temperature computed over 7 temperatures). Nothing tests temperature, retry or model choice on the generic-space step; KOMBINE reports only temperature 0.9.
agent_test: Sweep temperature 0.3, 0.7, 1.0 and best-of-N with a check, at equal tokens, on the generic-frame step; report valid-frame rate.

claim: No study compares a structured blend step against a plain 'combine A and B' prompt at equal tokens with a human or code-checked outcome. The nearest is a single-case protocol vs brainstorming comparison (74/80 vs 49/80, AI judge, author rubric, tokens unmatched, 7 of 8 batch successes with no baseline).
agent_test: Run plain, structured (generic frame then blend then check) and best-of-N arms at equal tokens on random pairs; score by code check plus a blind human sample.

claim: No published code check of a generic frame has measured agreement with humans. The closest published check is a typed-structure gate (preservation rate below 0.30 rejected; 13,951 gate-passed, 163 cross-domain judged, 9 survivors; about 17:1 filtering) whose authors have not measured false negatives against human grades. Their LLM judge runs fail-open and its six axes separate 154 rejected from 9 survivors.
agent_test: Build a three-part code check (frame non-empty, both inputs covered, emergent property absent from both input lists) and compare with two human raters on 100 blends.

claim: Cross-domain recombination and analogical reuse have shown gains on task outcomes, but none of these tests a blend operator. Thought Propagation (analogy): +12% shortest-path optimality, +15% agent planning completion (abstract). Discovery by Dreaming (training): GSM8K +14.5 pp, 95% CI +9.8 to +18.7 on the full test at rank 256, but putting the same material in context to a 671B model did not reproduce the gain and reversed it.
agent_test: Measure the blend operator on a gold-answer task (ARC-like or a design puzzle) with and without the blend step at equal tokens.

claim: Novel combinations are one place where LLM agreement with humans may rest on shallow cues: GPT-3's interpretations of novel noun compounds closely match human patterns (Exp 1), but when nonce words carry the artifact or natural-kind category (Exp 3) there is no convincing evidence it reasons beyond individual lexical items (Li, Carlson and Potts 2022). On CCPT, humans score 49.2 on emergent property induction, 38.0 on noun-phrase completion, and 81% on property-type accuracy.
agent_test: Never accept a model's own rating of a novel blend; require an external check against the input property lists.
audit_note: Only Li et al. and CCPT are listed; neither supports the sentence that embedding models track human plausibility of novel-compound paraphrases less well (older models better), and neither shows LLMs follow humans 'least' on novel combinations. Li et al. found a high GPT-3 match to humans (Exp 1) but no convincing evidence of reasoning beyond lexical items (Exp 3); human CCPT figures 49.2/38.0/81% are right.
claim_before_audit: Novel and unusual combinations are where LLMs follow humans least. Embedding models track human plausibility of compound paraphrases much less for novel compounds (older models do better); GPT-3 matches human compound interpretation but fails when nonce words carry the category (Experiment 3). Humans on CCPT: emergent induction 49.2, noun-phrase completion 38.0, property-type accuracy 81%.

claim: Several requested sources stayed unread or unfound: Gibbs 2000, Coulson and Matlock 2001, McCubbins and Turner 2013 and Eppe 2018 (paywalled), Estes and Ward 2002 and Wilkenfeld and Ward 2001 (abstract or second-hand only), any LLM test of Fauconnier and Turner optimality principles as a score, any expert case study showing an explicit generic-space step, and any direct replication of Hampton's emergence counts after 2010.
agent_test: Treat as open; do not cite numbers for these.
